documentation.range:
Saiga once inhabited the steppes and semi-desert regions of south-eastern Europe, across Central Asia to Mongolia and north-west China, but the original range has been greatly reduced. In the 18th century the range of the Saiga extended across the south-eastern steppes of Europe from the north-west side of the Caspian to the foothills of the Carpathians, at about 25 °E (Heptner et al. 1961). The European range covered the territories of modern-day Russia, Ukraine, Moldova, and probably the eastern part of Romania. Early reports of Saiga occurrence in Poland refer to the historic borders in the mid-1800s (Heptner et al. 1961) and the species has never been recorded within the current territory of Poland. The former European range has been greatly reduced. Saiga became extinct in Moldova and Ukraine in the 18th century, and by the 1920s-1930s the European range was restricted to the Kalmyk steppes (Heptner et al. 1961). Saiga disappeared from China in the middle of the 20th century (Cui et al. 2017). In 1958 the global range covered an estimated 2.5 million km² (Heptner et al. 1961).

There are five main Saiga populations: one in Russia (North-West pre-Caspian), three predominantly in Kazakhstan (Ural, Ustiurt, Betpak-dala), and one in Mongolia. The principal Russian population occurs in the steppes north-west of the Caspian Sea in Kalmykia and adjoining parts of Astrakhan Region. Beginning in 2015, small numbers of Saiga began to be seen in Orenburg State Reserve, and also in the Saratov, Volgograd, and Astrakhan provinces, having dispersed from the expanding Ural population in Kazakhstan. In 2018-2021 numbers in these parts of Russia increased when the region was impacted by a series of droughts. This population is seasonal, from around April to September; very few remain in winter, except for a small sedentary population around Lake Bulukhta (Smelyansky et al. 2022/2023). However as the Ural population in Kazakhstan increases, dispersal may result in Saiga numbers in the Russian part of the range also increasing and more becoming permanently resident.

The three Kazakhstan populations are located in Ural in the north-west (which is partially transboundary with Russia), Betpak-dala in central Kazakhstan, and Ustyurt in the south. Animals from the Ustyurt population migrate south in winter into Uzbekistan, in some years reaching Turkmenistan, returning in spring. These transboundary movements have declined in range and frequency and no Saiga have not been seen in Turkmenistan for several years. The number reaching Uzbekistan has also declined, further limited by construction of a border fence. There is a small outlying population east of the main Betpak-dala population, in the Semipalatinsk region.

The nominate subspecies also formerly occurred in the Dzungarian Gobi of far south-western Mongolia and is assumed to have been a transboundary population with China, but became extinct in the 1960s. The Mongolian subspecies S. t. mongolica occurs in western Mongolia, north of the Altai mountains, which separate its range from the nominate subpopulations. Mongolian Saiga once occurred through the Great Lakes Basin from the north-west corner, east to approximately 101°E (Bannikov 1954), but both range and numbers became severely reduced. In the 1980s the range was small, and centred on Shargiin Gobi and Khuisiin Gobi with a small satellite population in Mankhan soum (district). The range expanded during the 1990s-2000s as a result of favourable climatic conditions and Saiga have now occupied Dorgon Tal, and Khomiin Tal (east of Khar Nuur), and moved north into Uvs aimag (province). The area of distribution in Khaliun and Sharga districts has also expanded. The Mankhan subpopulation has also extended its range but is still isolated from the core populations. The current northern limit is about 48030’N and eastern limit about 95030’E. Saiga are still absent from the eastern part of their historic range in the Lakes Valley (Biger Nuur, Boon Tsagaan Nuur, Orog Nuur).
documentation.population:
Historically, herds may have numbered in the millions, however counting methods were unreliable until the introduction of robust methods in several of the populations from the 2000s. Excessive hunting reduced Saiga numbers to an estimated total of ca. 1,000 by the early 20th century (Heptner et al. 1961) though the accuracy of this estimate is unclear. The species received legal protection in 1919 and soon began to recover. By 1960 Saiga numbers had reached an estimated 540,000 in Russia and 1,300,000 in Kazakhstan (Linnard 1963). Commercial harvests resumed in the 1950s and continued until 1990. There were still an estimated 1,250,000 Saiga in the mid-1970s.

In Russia, the Saiga population steeply declined along with land reclamation of the Volga basin, but the species remained numerous. In the 1970s the population recovered to ca. 700,000-800,000 as a result of hunting regulations. In 1980 there were an estimated 380,000 individuals, in 1996 there were 196,000, but by the year 2000 just 26,000 (see Milner-Gulland et al. 2001 for annual survey results for 1980–2000).

Saiga numbers fell catastrophically from 1989 on, when political and economic changes accompanying the break-up of the USSR led to weakening of nature protection systems and severe economic hardship, while at the same time, international borders were opened up, enhancing the opportunities for trading Saiga horn (Mallon 2016b and references therein). Poaching for horns surged and large numbers were killed locally for meat. The largest population of Saiga fell to 4% of its estimated 1990 size and other populations also suffered large reductions (Milner-Gulland et al. 2001). Evidence from Russia indicated that selective harvesting had left a skewed population containing few adult males, many females without young, and the population close to reproductive collapse (Milner-Gulland et al. 2003). The full scale of the catastrophic decline was detailed by Arylov et al. (2004). Numbers in Kazakhstan fell to only 21,000 in 2003. The species was assessed as Critically Endangered in 2002.

A wide range of conservation measures was implemented and Saiga numbers stabilized then increased (Milner-Gulland 2010). The largest population, in Betpakdala, Kazakhstan, grew by 76% annually during 2003 and 2010, demonstrating the resilience of the species. However, poaching and other factors reduced Saiga numbers in Russia and caused a 47% decrease in Ustyurt during 2009-2010. In May 2010 a disease outbreak killed ca 12,000 Saiga in the Ural population, a 31% loss. Nevertheless, numbers continued to grow overall and by spring 2015 there were >300,000 Saiga in Kazakhstan, plus a few thousand each in in Russia and Mongolia. Then in September 2015 a mass die-off occurred in Betpakdala, the largest population, with at least 200,000 dying in the course of three weeks, representing >80% of that population and >60% of the global population (Milner-Gulland 2015, Kock et al. 2018).

The population in Kazakhstan has recovered dramatically, growing by about 1100% between 2015 and 2022, and showing annual increases up to 40%. The aerial census in May 2022 estimated a total of 1,320,000 Saiga in Kazakhstan (801,000 in Ural, 479,000 in Betpak-dala, 28,000 in Ustyurt) (Anon. 2022/2023). The size of the Ural population is now higher than at any time in recent memory.

In Russia, a survey in 2020 by WWF-Russia using drones estimated 6,350 in the NW Caspian population (Safronova et al. 2022/2023). There are an estimated 4000 resident Saiga around Lake Bulukhta and in 2020 around 28,000-33,000 occurred seasonally in the Trans-Volga region (Smelyansky et al. 2022/23). A small population in eastern Kazakhstan not covered by the annual surveys may number around 2,000.

Dash et al. (1977) estimated only 200 Mongolian Saiga. That population reached ca. 3,000 in 1998 and 5,200 in 2000, helped by favourable climatic conditions and active conservation measures. Numbers fell again between 2000 and 2002 as a result of severe winters and summer drought. The decline continued in 2002–2003, mainly because of poaching. Estimated numbers were 1,020 in 2003, and 750 in January 2004. However, numbers then increased steadily to ca. 11,000 in 2016, when an outbreak of peste de petits ruminants (PPR) killed around 54% of the population. This population has also now recovered. The annual survey by WWF-Mongolia in November 2022 estimated 13,925, a 38.2% increase on the previous year (Chimeddorj 2022/2023a).
The global Saiga population in March 2023 is therefore estimated to number about 1,344,275 (ca 1,008,200 mature individuals). Numbers in all current populations are increasing, albeit at different rates and with different levels of uncertainty around the estimates (CMS 2021).

Counts made using appropriate methods (aerial surveys with strip sampling in Kazakhstan, ground surveys with distance sampling in Mongolia) enable precision of the count to be estimated, and reduce, but do not eliminate, bias. Expert assessments, as carried out in Russia and Uzbekistan, are prone to unquantifiable levels of bias. For wide-ranging ungulates such as the Saiga, even well-conducted counts are likely to be underestimates, and the degree of underestimation increases as population gets smaller and more fragmented, because the animals are harder to detect. This means that population declines may appear worse, and increases faster, than they really are (McConville et al. 2008).
documentation.habitats:
The Saiga is a nomadic herding species that inhabits open dry steppe grasslands and semi-arid deserts of Central Asia. Typical habitat consists of flat open areas covered with low-growing vegetation, allowing animals to run quickly; areas of broken terrain or dense cover are generally avoided, but animals may stray into these out of necessity or shelter in them during strong winds, they range from near or below sea level in the Caspian basin to ca 1,600 m in Mongolia (Heptner et al. 1961, Bekenov et al. 1998).

Saiga are migratory, with most populations having widely separated summer (northern) and winter (southern) ranges. S. t. mongolica is not migratory. The NW Caspian population no longer migrates and the Ural population makes limited seasonal movements. The species lives in large herds, usually up to thousands of individuals. It has a high rate of reproduction and recruitment since females usually breed at 7-8 months and males in their second year (Heptner et al. 1961) and females often bear twins. In years with a favourable climate the population can increase by up to 60% in a single year (Chan et al. 1995). Very few animals in a population are more than 3.5 years old, indicating that the population is almost completely renewed after four years (Bekenov et al. 1998). Males defend a harem of 5-10 females and gestation lasts about 5 months (Heptner et al. 1961). Saiga are grazers and have been recorded feeding on a wide range of grasses and herbaceous plant species.

For full details of the biology of the species see Heptner et al. (1961) and Sokolov and Zhirnov (1998).
documentation.threats:
Saiga are susceptible to several diseases, including foot-and-mouth disease, brucellosis, and others, which can cause large numbers of deaths (Robinson 2018). There have been four recent mass-mortality events MME). In 2010, around two-thirds of a calving aggregation of 20,000 in the Ural population died of a peracute respiratory disease with bloat, and this was followed in 2011 by a smaller die-off of several hundreds of Saiga with similar clinical signs, immediately after calving, and grazing in the exact same location as the earlier MME, suggesting a site-specific cause. Pasteurellosis was implicated based on bacteriology, but very little pathology was undertaken and the clinical signs were more aligned with fog fever or bloat, caused by an excess of protein-rich grass (Kock et al. 2018, Robinson et al. 2019).

In 2015, more than 200,000 Saiga died within three weeks in central Kazakhstan. The proximate cause of death, based on multiple strands of evidence, was confirmed as haemorrhagic septicaemia caused by the bacterium Pasteurella multocida type B (Kock et al. 2018, Robinson et al. 2019). Statistical modelling suggests that there was unusually high relative humidity and temperature in the days leading up to the outbreak; temperature and humidity anomalies were also observed in two previous similar events in the same region. The modelled influence of environmental covariates is consistent with known drivers of haemorrhagic septicemia. Given the Saiga population’s vulnerability to mass mortality and the likely exacerbation of climate-related and environmental stressors in the future, management of risks to population viability, such as poaching and viral livestock disease, is urgently needed, as well as robust ongoing veterinary surveillance (Kock et al. 2018).

On 22nd December 2016 the first death of a Mongolian Saiga (S. t. mongolica) was reported by herders to the local authorities in Darvi soum (district) in the Khuisiin Gobi. Hundreds of live and dead Saiga were subsequently observed with a PPR-like signs. Samples were confirmed at the Mongolia State Central Veterinary Laboratory (SCVL) on 6th January 2017 to contain PPR virus and gene sequencing confirmed the virus to be highly similar to the virus recorded in sheep and goats. The Saiga infection developed rapidly into a full-blown epidemic and by the end of January; death and infection were reported across most of Mongolian Saiga range (Kock 2017). Based on carcass counts, over 54% of the population is estimated to have died. PPR is spreading through Central Asia, and infects a range of wild and domestic ungulate species, with the reservoir hosts being sheep and goats. Saigas appear to be uniquely susceptible to high levels of mortality from this disease (Pruvot et al. 2020).

Saiga share many parasites with livestock, and in the past have been severely affected by some of these parasites (e.g. the Mongolian saiga gadfly that went extinct when saiga numbers were at their lowest levels in the 1920s). The presence of parasites generally does not cause mortality, but could interact with other factors such as climate change to reduce survival (Khanyari et al. 2022).

Uncontrolled hunting for horns and meat caused the first major decline in saiga in the early 20th century. A surge in poaching for the horns of the males following the break-up of the former USSR in the late 1980s-early 1990s also led to a catastrophic fall in Saiga numbers. Selective hunting of males and subsequent distortion of the sex ratio further affected reproduction by heavily skewing the sex ratio (Milner-Gulland et al. 2003). Evidence from Russia indicated that selective harvesting had left a skewed population containing few adult males, many females without young, and the population close to reproductive collapse (Milner-Gulland et al. 2003). Extensive anti-poaching measures have been implemented, along with education programmes, training for customs and border officials, and action in end-user countries, resulting in a reduction in poaching and trade. This situation is entirely dependent on stringent enforcement and any relaxation of existing efforts can be expected to cause an upsurge in illegal killing and trade.

Extreme climatic events pose a threat, both summer droughts and severe winters, especially a set of conditions known as dzuud or dzhut when heavy prolonged heavy snow cover, sustained very low temperatures, and/or an ice-crust preventing access to forage. During harsh winters, Saiga mortality in local populations can be up to 50%, followed by recovery in the next 2-3 years (Bekenov et al. 1998. The potential impacts of climate change on Saiga populations are poorly understood at present and modelling and vulnerability assessments are needed to better understand these.

Loss or degradation of steppe habitats due to conversion for agriculture and overgrazing, as well as competition with livestock have affected some parts of the range. The Saiga population in eastern Kalmkyia, Russia, co-exists with very high numbers of sheep and goats (1,328,300 in 2019; Smelyansky et al. 2022/2023). Regular steppe fires pose an additional threat to the habitat in Kalmykia (Shinkarenko and Berdengalieva 2022/2023). although fires in moderation may promote flushes of vegetation on which Saiga preferentially graze.
In Ural, the rapidly growing Saiga population is causing increasing concern about by local communities over damage to crops, competition for pasture and water, and concern about disease transmission. In Mongolia, livestock grazing pressure and competition with livestock are high, and habitat is reported as severely fragmented. The Saiga's main water sources are seasonally occupied by herders and their livestock, limiting access and causing damage.

Linear infrastructure (railways, roads, pipelines, and a border fence) are impacting Saiga populations, particularly Ustyurt and Betpak-dala, and these negative impacts will increase with upcoming infrastructure projects, unless mitigation measures are implemented (CMS 2021).

The unprecedented increase in the size of the Ural population in Kazakhstan (801,000 in May 2022) has led to complaints from farmers in the region of damage to crops. A conservation and management strategy for the Ural population has been developed in response (CMS 2023).

The European population specifically is threatened by the current geopolitical isolation of Russia, such that international conservation support, funding and networking cannot include this population at the moment. For example, in 2022, the USFWS funded a portfolio of projects on saiga conservation along the trade supply chain, aiming to produce the evidence base underpinning transformative change towards sustainability. These projects go from on-the-ground actions in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Mongolia, to stockpile management in Thailand and consumer demand in Japan, Singapore and China. The European saiga population is not part of this portfolio as funding from most overseas sources  cannot be directed at conservation in Russia at the moment.

Finally, the low levels of genetic diversity found in all Saiga populations (Rey-Iglesia et al. 2022) potentially reduce the capacity of the species to adapt to emerging diseases and environmental changes.
documentation.measures:
Saiga are protected in all range states but the level of enforcement varies. Anti-poaching efforts in Kazakhstan and other countries have been intensified over the last 10 years.

Saiga are listed on the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) Appendix II and the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) Appendix II. The CMS Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) Concerning Conservation, Restoration and Sustainable Use of the Saiga Antelope came into effect in 2006 and has been signed by all five range states and ten Cooperating Organizations (local and international NGOs). The MoU has an associated Medium-Term International Work Programme (MTIWP) setting out a framework for conservation action by all partners. Technical coordination for the MOU is undertaken by the Saiga Conservation Alliance and Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan in close collaboration with the CMS Secretariat. The MTIWP is reviewed and updated periodically at technical workshops preceding CMS MoU range state meetings. In April 2019, a joint CMS-CITES technical workshop was held on Vilm Island, Germany, where a revised Medium Term International Work Programme for 2021-2025 was drafted and later approved by the range states.

Since 2002 both CMS and CITES have worked in close cooperation, with Saiga as one of their joint target species. The CMS-CITES Joint Work Programme 2015-2020, adopted at the 42nd meeting of the CMS Standing Committee and the 65th  meeting of the CITES Standing Committee, outlines the current joint activities on Saiga. These focus on the implementation of the MTIWP, joint meetings and fundraising efforts (CMS 2021).

At CITES COP18 in August 2019 the following decisions related to Saiga were adopted (Decisions 18.270-274). 1. To direct Range States, important consumer and trading countries to implement the CMS Medium-Term International Work Programme for the Saiga Antelope for 2016-2020 and for 2021-2025; 2. To encourage the range States to establish internal market controls for Saiga parts (including registration of stockpiles, labelling of parts and products, and registration of manufacturers and traders). 3. Subject to funding, the CITES Secretariat should consult with, and support, Range States and major consumer and trading states to manage their stockpiles and improve stockpile management. 4. CITES Parties also adopted a zero quota for wild specimens traded for commercial purposes, which entered into force on 16th November 2019 (CMS 2021).
A conservation and management strategy for the Ural population has been developed in respone to concerns from farmers that the expanding population was damaging crops (CMS 2023).

Population Monitoring
In Kazakhstan a comprehensive monitoring programme covers nearly all of Saiga range. Since 2016, spring surveys of all three populations have been conducted using a standard methodology comprising aerial and ground surveys. Kazakhstan has also started implementing the SMART monitoring system for rangers. In Russia, aerial surveys using drones have been trialled. Ground-based monitoring by staff of the Chernye Zemli Biosphere Reserve and Stepnoi Sanctuary provides expert assessments, supplemented by opportunistic monitoring to give information on distribution and herd sizes outside these reserves. In Uzbekistan, a combination of participatory monitoring using motorbike transects and ground surveys gives a general impression of population change. In Mongolia, a comprehensive aerial survey was carried out in 2009/2010, and rangewide population monitoring using the distance sampling line transect approaches has been carried out annually since 2011, led by WWF-Mongolia. A Saiga ranger network carries out monthly monitoring and patrolling in core Saiga areas since 2015, and has been using SMART since July 2019 to improve effectiveness and support systematic data collection (CMS 2021).

Protected areas
The distance between summer and winter ranges of some populations hinders full protected area coverage. In Russia, most Saiga are found in Chernye Zemli Biosphere Reserve (5,842 km²), established in 1990, and the adjoining Stepnoi Sanctuary (1,090 km²). Saiga are seasonally present in summer in Elton Nature Park (1,056 km²), Baskunchak Nature Park (395 km²), Orenberg reserve (382 km²), and Bogdinsko-Baskunchakskiy State Nature Reserve (185 km²).

In Kazakhstan the Irgiz-Turgai Sanctuary (7,635 km²), Altyn Dala State Nature Reserve (4,897 km²), Korgalzhyn Reserve (5,431 km²), Naurzum Reserve (1,913 km²) and Barsalemess Reserve (1,608 km²)  have been established to protect Saiga populations. In May 2022 the Government of Kazakhstan gazetted the Bokeyorda State Nature Reserve (3,430 km²) and Ashiozek State Wildlife Sanctuary (3,145 km²) to protect the Ural population in West Kazakhstan province  (Smelyansky and Koshkina 2022/2023). In Uzbekistan the Saigachy Sanctuary was redesignated in 2015 to provide better coverage of Saiga range and now covers 8,481 km².

The Mongolian Saiga has been legally protected since 1953 and occur in the following protected areas: Sharga-Mankhan Nature Reserve (3,962 km²), Khomyn Tal NP (4,111 km²), Khar-Us Nuur  NP (8,530 km²), Khyargas Lake NP (3,413 km²), Mongol Els NP (2,030 km²), Khar Azargiin Nuruu NR (1,926 km²), Bukhun Local protected Area (1,697 km²).  Since January 2021, three more Local Protected Areas have been designated, covering 2,581 km². A total of 56.1% of Mongolian saiga range is now protected by both State Protected Areas (29.4%) and Local Protected Areas (26.7%) (Chimeddorj 2022/2023b).

Captive breeding
Small groups of Saiga have been kept in zoos in Europe and the USA but the species is difficult to maintain in captivity. Small rescue and captive breeding centres exist in Russia and Kazakhstan. A workshop to review options for Saiga captive breeding and reintroduction took place in Moscow in August 2017 (SCA, SDZG, IEEM 2017). At that time, there were c. 907 Saiga in eight captive or semi-captive facilities: 117 in four facilities in Russia; 20 at two facilities in Kazakhstan; 170 at the Wuwei Breeding Centre in Gansu, China; and c. 600 at the Askania Nova centre in Ukraine. There is no captive breeding currently in Uzbekistan. The population in Wuwei crashed to about 20 by early 2019. About 600 Saiga in Askania Nova, Ukraine, are kept in extensive semi-captive conditions and live animals have been sold in recent years to raise income to fund the centre. The status of these animals since the start of the conflict in 2022 is unknown (CMS 2021).

Other projects
The Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative in Kazakhstan is a collaboration between international and national NGOs and national and regional governmental bodies, which aims to provide an integrated approach to planning an implementation of sustainable land management, with the Saiga as its focal species. The initiative expanded its area of operations in 2016 to include the Ural and Ustyurt populations in addition to Betpakdala, and the project area now covers about 75 million ha.

The Saiga Conservation Alliance (SCA) is a network of researchers and conservationists formed in 2016 to study and protect the saiga antelope. SCA maintains the online Saiga Resource Centre and publishes Saiga News one or twice a year (in English, Russian, Kazakh, Uzbek, Mongolian, and Chinese). It also provides small grants for research and awards for saiga protection and young conservationists.

Saiga Day is an international initiative developed by SCA as a focus for rural communities to promote conservation of Saiga and its habitat. It takes take place each spring to mark the birth of the first Saiga calves of the year.

The ‘Resurrection Island’ programme in Uzbekistan aims to lay the foundation for designating Resurrection Island in Uzbekistan as a Protected Area for Saiga and other species, while developing sustainable income streams for local enabling residents. It is a collaboration between the Uzbekistan government, industry, in-country NGOs, and the University of Oxford.

In March 2023, the SCA hosted a ‘Saiga Inception’ meeting and ‘Conserving Wildlife in the Central Asian Steppes’ panel event in Oxford. These events brought together participants from different projects in the saiga antelope range, supported by the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s new 5-year “Catalysing Conservation Fund”, which focussed on generating evidence on Saiga product trade chains. The meeting aimed to facilitate collaboration among Saiga projects and address key aspects such as data availability, evidence gaps, theory of change, capacity needs, and opportunities for shared learning. The meeting brought together representatives from various organisations, including the CMS Central Asian Mammals Initiative, United States Fish and Wildlife Service, Oxford University, Zoological Society of London, Wildlife Conservation Society, Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, Flora and Fauna International, TRAFFIC, Frankfurt Zoological Society, The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds, and other international and national stakeholders.
documentation.use_trade: The horns of male Saiga are highly valued in Traditional Asian Medicine (Chan et al. 1995), while meat and hides have been used in saiga range states for centuries.  A legal harvest, predominately for meat, with fixed quotas operated from the 1950s to 1990. These harvests were formerly conducted on an industrial scale, using trucks , each with a team of up to 20 hunters. For example, west of the Volga River, 120,000–150,000 Saiga were harvested per year during 1957–1962 (Linnard 1963). A recent study in Singapore demonstrated high levels of use of saiga-containing products (19% of Chinese Singaporeans reported using it as their main medication for ‘heatiness’ in 2019; Doughty et al. 2019). Both China and Singapore have reported stockpiles of several tons of Saiga horn each. Meat is eaten locally and traded within the range. All aspects of sustainable use of Saiga are considered in a recent report (Milner-Gulland et al. 2020).
documentation.rationale:
Saiga is assessed as Near Threatened because of extreme data uncertainty which makes an assessment as Endangered, Vulnerable, or Least Concern equally plausible.

The previous assessment considered that Saiga crossed the threshold between Critically Endangered and Endangered in May 2015 and met Endangered under criterion A4 based on an observed, estimated, and projected decline of more than 50% over 11 years (three generations), commencing in May 2015, due to the risk of mass mortality events (MME) from outbreaks of disease, severe climate, and poaching for the illegal trade in horns. Under the 5-year rule, a reassessment was due in 2020.

Numbers in Kazakhstan, which holds more than 98% of the global Saiga population, have recovered dramatically, increasing by about 1,100% between 2015 and 2022 and showing annual increases of up to 40%, necessitating a reappraisal. The total population size in Kazakhstan was estimated at 1,320,000 in May 2022, and there are a further ca. 20,000 in Russia and Mongolia.
 
Saiga are susceptible to a range of infectious diseases, including foot-and-mouth disease, brucellosis, and others, and their occurrence in large herds makes them liable to large-scale die-offs. Four major disease outbreaks since 2010 have caused mass mortality events (MME). The most severe outbreak caused the death of over 200,000 Saiga in one population in Kazakhstan over the course of three weeks in May 2015. The cause of this outbreak (and the suspected cause in the earlier two) has been shown to be haemorrhagic septicaemia possibly caused by the bacterium Pasteurella multocida. The most recent MME occurred in the Mongolian saiga population in early 2017, caused by peste de petits ruminants (PPR), when an estimated 54% of the population died.

PPR is relatively new to the region, but is still spreading through Central Asia, posing a threat to all saiga populations. Pasteurella is endemic in Saiga, and the high lethal levels of mortality implicated in the Kazakhstan MMEs are believed to have been triggered by environmental conditions including abnormally high humidity and temperature. Warm and wet climatic conditions are expected to increase in frequency due to effects of recorded and predicted climate change. Given the Saiga’s inherent vulnerability to disease, likely exacerbated by climate-related and environmental stressors in the future, and the expanding interface between domestic livestock and Saiga across their global range which increases the risks of disease transfer, the risk of disease outbreaks causing significant mortality remains very high.

The species is also threatened by climatic factors, poaching, and habitat degradation. Severe winter conditions known as dzhut or dzuud, consisting of heavy snowfall, sustained, very cold temperatures, and/or an ice crust preventing access to forage, are also known to cause high mortality in Saiga. Poaching for the international illegal trade in horns and local illegal trade in meat is a constant threat and requires the current stringent controls to be maintained. Local pressures include competition with livestock, overgrazing, steppe fires, drought, and damage to natural springs.

The most severe recent MME killed around 80% of one population in Kazakhstan in 2015. Using an 11-year (three generation) window starting in 2020, a new disease outbreak on the same scale and resulting in the same level of mortality in the largest current population (801,000), would result in a reduction of the global population of 52%. A less lethal outbreak could cause a population reduction of 30–50%. These scenarios would justify a category of Endangered or Vulnerable, respectively, under criterion A4e.

However, it is now clear that the rapid recent population increases resulted in full recovery of the affected population within a few years of the MME occurrence, and certainly in less than 11 years. If these population growth rates were to continue, Saiga would not meet the thresholds for either Endangered or Vulnerable for the full duration of the 3-generation window, in which case, Least Concern would apply.

There are several caveats:
1. Saiga population increases on this scale over almost a decade are unprecedented and may not be sustained for demographic or environmental reasons (e.g. a sequence of severe winter conditions or summer droughts).
2. The timing, location, severity, and frequency of MMEs is unpredictable and the possibility of a more lethal MME, simultaneous MMEs in more than one Saiga population, or consecutive MMEs within the same time-window cannot be discounted.
3. An upsurge in poaching (e.g. due to relaxation of protection efforts, and/or an increase in the market price for Saiga horn) could exacerbate the effects of an MME, hinder recovery, or cause a substantial population reduction on its own.

In view of the multiple unpredictable factors, and the potential interplay between them, the Endangered, Vulnerable, and Least Concern categories are all considered to be equally plausible, amounting to considerable and genuine data uncertainty. Saiga is therefore assessed as Near Threatened.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Saiga tatarica is the only species in the genus Saiga. Two subspecies are recognised by IUCN: Saiga tatarica tatarica (to which the European and the majority of the global population belongs), and Saiga tatarica mongolica, endemic to western Mongolia. Mongolian Saiga was first described as a separate species, Saiga mongolica by Bannikov (1946) based on differences in skull measurements, shape and size of horns, and colour of pelage. However, the author later revised his opinion and considered it to be only a subspecies (Bannikov 1954).

Grubb (2005) recognized the Pleistocene mammoth-steppe Saiga as a distinct species S. borealis, following Baryshnikov and Tikhonov (1994) and included the living subspecies mongolica. However, a later analysis of mtDNA from 93 tissue samples from all five extant Saiga populations confirmed that S. tatarica mongolica is genetically distinct, whereas the four populations of the nominate subspecies are polyphyletic, consistent with recent fragmentation and population declines; there were clear but only slight differences between S. t. mongolica and S. t. tatarica, confirming the designation of S. t. mongolica as a subspecies rather than a species (Kholodova et al. 2006).

Campos et al. (2010) analysed modern and fossil Saiga using mtDNA from 27 ancient and 38 modern specimens from all parts of Saiga range, including two specimens of putative S. borealis. The results showed two distinct lineages, the first including all modern and fossil Saiga from north-east Yakutia and the Urals, the second occurring only in the northern Urals and now extinct. Campos et al. (2010) concluded that: “...the data suggest that S. borealis does not constitute a distinct subspecies or species”. Furthermore, the authors of this 2010 study include both Baryshnikov and Tikhonov, the co-authors of the 1994 paper, and who are therefore regarded as supporting this revised view (Mallon 2016a).

Rey-Iglesia et al. (2022) sequenced the mitochondrial control region and 19 microsatellite markers of both subspecies. The result revealed low genetic diversity and low levels of heterozygosity for both S. t. mongolica (He = 0.325, Ho = 0.290) and S. t. tatarica subspecies (He = 0.215, Ho = 0.313 for Kalmykia and He = 0.274, Ho = 0.365 for Kazakhstan). The microsatellite data indicated a single population (K = 1) and therefore no structure at nuclear level between the two subspecies. This lack of genetic structure may indicate reduced time since separation of the two forms or low resolution due to the small number of S. t. tatarica samples. Increased sampling effort and a higher number of nuclear markers, ideally using genomic information, are necessary to adequately elucidate the genetic structure of the subspecies (Rey-Iglesia et al. 2022).
